t:
Section 890 of title 10, United States Code (article 90 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice), is amended to read as follows:“§ 890. Art. 90. Willfully disobeying superior commissioned officer  “Any person subject to this chapter who willfully disobeys a lawful command of that person’s superior commissioned officer shall be punished—“(1) if the offense is committed in time of war, by death or such other punishment as a court-martial may direct; and“(2) if the offense is committed at any other time, by such punishment, other than death, as a court-martial may direct.”
.

fable.w: This section defines a military criminal offense and its punishments under the UCMJ. A tempting reading treats the court-martial as a hearing, but that is an internal military adjudication of an individual's offense, not consultation with outside parties before a federal policy decision. No comment period, rulemaking, advisory body, outside consultation, or right to sue is provided.
fable.s: Any person subject to this chapter who willfully disobeys a lawful command of that person’s superior commissioned officer shall be punished

qwen_block.w: This section defines a criminal offense (willfully disobeying a superior officer) and establishes the penalties for that offense within the military justice system. It does not involve consultation, coordination, or participation by parties outside the federal government in a decision-making process. The actors involved (superior officers, court-martial) are all part of the federal government/military structure.
qwen_block.s: Any person subject to this chapter who willfully disobeys a lawful command of that person’s superior commissioned officer shall be punished—(1) if the offense is committed in time of war, by death or such other punishment as a court-martial may direct; and (2) if the offense is committed at any other time, by such punishment, other than death, as a court-martial may direct.

opus.w: This section redefines a criminal offense under the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ) and its punishments. The reference to a court-martial might look like a hearing, but a court-martial is a military tribunal inside the federal government, so no outside party takes part in any federal decision. The section has no consultation, comment period, advisory body or right to sue.
opus.s: Any person subject to this chapter who willfully disobeys a lawful command of that person’s superior commissioned officer shall be punished

qwen_chat.w: This section defines a criminal offense and its punishment within the Uniform Code of Military Justice. It does not involve consultation, coordination, or participation by parties outside the federal government in a decision-making process. Court-martials are internal military judicial proceedings, not public participation mechanisms.
qwen_chat.s: Any person subject to this chapter who willfully disobeys a lawful command of that person’s superior commissioned officer shall be punished—(1) if the offense is committed in time of war, by death or such other punishment as a court-martial may direct; and (2) if the offense is committed at any other time, by such punishment, other than death, as a court-martial may direct.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that a court-martial involves "participation" because it is a hearing where the accused can present evidence. However, a court-martial is a judicial proceeding within the military justice system, not a participatory process for outside parties to influence a federal administrative or policy decision. The accused is a member of the military (inside the government structure for this purpose) or subject to military jurisdiction, and the process is adjudicative, not consultative. Furthermore, the text itself only defines the punishment, not the procedural rights of the accused.
